1966 to 2026

The complete timeline

Every sourced entry in the archive, 1540 of them, in the order they happened, with the 2318 unworked lines from the Herald index kept separate under the year they belong to. 399 of the entries are things student government put on for the campus, and the filter above will show only those. Jump to a year below, or read one decade at a time.

1960s 1970s 1980s 1990s 2000s 2010s 2020s The complete timeline

Entries are the archive’s own record: each one is dated, written up and carries the source it rests on. The grey blocks under a year hold index lines from the digitised Herald that have been recorded but not yet worked into the record.

1966-67

Jim Haynes (president)

17 entries · 29 index lines

April 1966

President Kelly Thompson approves the constitution

The proposed constitution of the Associated Students of Western Kentucky University was completed in late March and approved on 1 April. The copy held by WKU Archives is dated 7 April 1966.

In the recordTopSCHOLAR - SGA Constitution

April 1966

Thompson's approval letter is addressed to committee chair Reed Morgan

The archived copy of Thompson's approval letter names the organizing committee that drafted the constitution: Reed Morgan as chair, John Lovett as vice chair. Morgan's committee did the drafting; Jim Haynes was elected to lead the government it created six weeks later.

In the recordUA3/3/1, Letter to Organizational Committee for a Western Student Organization, 1 Apr 1966 PDF

26 April 1966

Students ratify the constitution, 1,812 to 726

A four-day referendum. 2,538 students voted - a larger raw turnout than most SGA elections have managed since.

In the recordWKU SGA history

18 May 1966

Jim Haynes elected first president

Seven weeks from presidential approval to a seated student president. Western Kentucky State College became Western Kentucky University on 16 June, so the university and its student government are almost exactly the same age.

In the recordWKU SGA history

29 September 1966

The new government opens its first full year

The Herald's first issue of the fall reported the student senate ratifying a government appointment as the Associated Students began their first full academic year. Students had approved the constitution and elected officers the previous spring.

In the recordHerald 46:1, 29 Sep 1966 PDF

29 September 1966Programme

A state association floated as the route to better entertainment

The first Herald of the Associated Students' first full year carried an article headed "Campus Entertainment Improvements Possible Through State Association," the earliest sign of the block-booking idea that would define the organisation's entertainment work for the next decade.

In the recordHerald 46:1, 29 Sep 1966

27 October 1966

Doing well, but lacking communication

Midway through the fall semester the Herald judged that Associated Students leaders were performing well but were failing to communicate with the students they represented. It was the first public report card on the year-old government.

In the recordHerald 46:5, 27 Oct 1966 PDF

10 November 1966

Government and administration meet on campus problems

The Herald reported Student Government Association leaders meeting with President Kelly Thompson to discuss campus problems, an early instance of the year-old government dealing directly with the administration.

In the recordHerald 46:7, 10 Nov 1966 PDF

19 January 1967Service

A monthly events calendar posted outside the Associated Students office

The Herald reported that the month's campus events were being posted outside the Associated Students office. It is the earliest standing service the record shows the new government running for students.

In the recordHerald 46:12, 19 Jan 1967

9 March 1967

Herald warns of a 'popularity bandwagon' in the spring election

A week before the presidential campaign opened, the Herald ran a piece by Fran Salyers arguing that popularity, not merit, was set to decide the Associated Students election.

In the recordHerald 46:16, 9 Mar 1967 PDF

16 March 1967

Two vie for the presidency

The Herald reported two candidates seeking the Associated Students presidency, with campaigns for the organization's second presidential election set to open the following Monday.

In the recordHerald 46:17, 16 Mar 1967 PDF

6 April 1967Other

A student writes in wanting more entertainment

Tony Burdoc's letter, headed "Wants More Entertainment," ran in the Herald in April 1967, part of a running complaint about what the year-old government was putting on.

In the recordHerald 46:20, 6 Apr 1967

4 May 1967

Swearing-in set for May 10

The Herald announced that newly elected Associated Student officers would be sworn in on May 10, 1967, completing the organization's first full transfer of leadership.

In the recordHerald 46:22, 4 May 1967 PDF

12 May 1967

First year judged: organization, progress, apathy

Reviewing the government's first year, the Herald found organization and progress alongside persistent student apathy. The same issue carried president-elect William Menser's plans for 1967-68 and a letter arguing that the Associated Students really worked.

In the recordHerald 46:23, 12 May 1967 PDF

18 May 1967campus

Herald presses students to vote as the year closes

Days after the outgoing administration's year-end review, the Herald ran a piece headlined 'Goof Government Needs Student Vote,' pressing students toward greater turnout as Menser's incoming administration took over.

In the recordHerald 46:24, 18 May 1967 PDF

18 May 1967Other

The case for a student book exchange

Mark Dossey reported in the Herald that student book exchanges were working at Murray State and the University of Louisville, an argument for Western to run one of its own. Through the rest of the decade the exchange on this campus was run by the Veterans Club, not by the Associated Students.

In the recordHerald 46:24, 18 May 1967

30 May 1967

Dean Keown proposes a budget for the new government

Dean of Students Charles Keown sent President Kelly Thompson a memo proposing a student fee structure to create a budget for the Associated Student Government. He attached fee models gathered from universities across the South and Midwest.

In the recordUA3/3/1 Keown memo, 30 May 1967 PDF

1967-68

William Menser (president)

22 entries · 49 index lines

14 September 1967

Menser and President Thompson open the school year together

The first Herald of the 1967-68 year carried a joint welcome to students headlined "Dr. Kelly Thompson, William Menser Welcome Students." The same issue ran an item headed "Associated Student Government Events Set," laying out the organisation's calendar for the coming term.

In the recordHerald 47:1, 14 Sep 1967 PDF

14 September 1967Programme

The Associated Student Government sets its events for the year

The first Herald of 1967-68 announced the Associated Student Government's schedule of events for the coming year alongside the university's own lecture series and the Community Concerts season. It was the first year the government published a programme in advance.

In the recordHerald 47:1, 14 Sep 1967

The Herald reported that the student government had set new programmes for the year, in the same issue that announced Buckminster Fuller would lecture on campus and that Homecoming queen voting was set for Thursday.

1968-69

Reed Morgan (role unresolved) · Bill Straeffer (president) · Paul Gerard, III (student regent)

20 entries · 10 index lines

29 April 1968

Straeffer and Whitley vie for the presidency

The Herald's pre-election coverage set out the field: Bill Straeffer against Charles Whitley for president, Terry Gilpin against Bob Van Corbach for vice president, and contested races down to secretary, treasurer, and congressman at large.

In the recordHerald 47:28, 29 Apr 1968

2 May 1968

Straeffer elected president, 1,732 to 1,098; turnout 34 percent

The Associated Students' internal election-results memo lists the full slate: Bill Straeffer over Charles Whitley for president, Terry Gilpin over Bob Van Corbach for vice president, Becky Cooper over Mary Miller for secretary, Tonii Rizzo over John Combs for treasurer, and John Cobelli and Janie Heathcoat elected congressmen at large over Billy Goodman and Scott Phillips. Total turnout was 2,894 votes, about 34 percent of enrollment.

22 May 1969

President Kelly Thompson announces his resignation

Thompson, who had approved the Associated Students constitution in 1966, announced he would step down as WKU's president. The Herald covered it in the same issue as the incoming Zielke-Porter student administration.

Roger Miller announced the opening in the Herald under the headline "Another First: the Cellar, Associated Students Teahouse, Opens Friday." The paper covered it again a week later as "Cellar-Dwellers" and reported the campus teahouse stirred mixed emotions; by the end of April the Herald was calling it a dimly lit teahouse that outshone the government's other efforts. The 1972 Talisman describes it as a coffee house in West Hall.

In the recordHerald 51:28, 18 Jan 1972

25 January 1972Lecture

James J. Kilpatrick speaks

Reginald Glass announced in the Herald that the syndicated columnist James J. Kilpatrick would speak that night. The 1972 Talisman records him describing the youth vote as a real problem for the Republicans.

In the recordHerald 51:30, 25 Jan 1972

26 January 1972Film

The Associated Students movie series opens with King Kong

The Herald announced that the Associated Students movie series would open the next day with "King Kong," and an editorial three days later said the series could be a hit. The 1972 Talisman lists the Gaslight film series among the government's new entertainment; the Herald of 2 May had W. C. Fields in "The Flying Ace" set for Gaslight.

In the recordHerald 51:30, 25 Jan 1972

29 January 1972Concert

The Jake Jones mini-concert is cancelled

The Herald reported that the Associated Students had cancelled the Jake Jones mini-concert set for 29 January. The same issue carried a letter from Anthony Kinzel disconcerted with the government.

In the recordHerald 51:30, 25 Jan 1972

February 1972

'Student Regent May Get Vote'

Four years after the seat was created it was still non-voting. The same issue has the Academic Council clarifying grievance procedure and an Associated Students open session scheduled for 12 February.

In the recordHerald 51:32, 1 Feb 1972 PDF

4 February 1972Film

A cancelled Lennon and Ono screening brings a furious postbag

The Herald of 28 January had announced John Lennon and Yoko Ono films for the following week. On 4 February the paper printed three letters about the cancellation, one from a student who wanted to see the Lennon film and two headed "Disappointed at Film Cancellation" and "Furious at Film Cancellation," alongside Roger Miller reporting the Associated Students Congress reacting to censorship.

In the recordHerald 51:33, 4 Feb 1972

Norman Mailer lectures

Roger Miller announced in the Herald of 8 February that Norman Mailer's lecture was slated for the following night. The 1972 Talisman records the author and social critic telling his audience that amateurism was replacing professionalism.

In the recordHerald 51:34, 8 Feb 1972

15 February 1972Programme

Four sent to the entertainment conference

Jill Flanders reported that Reginald Glass, Mike Fiorella, Ron Beck and Jim Schmidt attended an entertainment conference. The 1972 Talisman explains the machinery behind the year's programme: Ron Beck was unit co-ordinator for the state branch of the National Entertainment Conference, ten schools were represented, the state body met on the Western campus in both semesters for programming workshops, and the three mini-concerts each semester were the result.

In the recordHerald 51:36, 15 Feb 1972

The Isaac Hayes concert is cancelled

Carter Pence reported the cancellation in the Herald of 18 February. The 1972 Talisman says the 17 February concert failed to materialise because Hayes was suffering from flu, and that he later contacted Western to reschedule.

Buffalo Bob Smith revives the Howdy Doody show in Van Meter

ASG brought Buffalo Bob Smith and his revival of the Howdy Doody show to Van Meter Auditorium in October 1972. The Talisman called the two-and-a-half hour programme professional and a huge success, with Smith leading a rendition of 'Clarabell the Clown' and playing Chopin, Mozart and Bach.

ASG presented Chicago on 4 October 1972 as a free concert, with pianist Robert Lamm fronting the horn section. The Talisman called it one of the season's hottest entertainment nights and said the band was soon forgotten once Jethro Tull arrived three weeks later.

a major financial loss for ASG, amount not stated

ASG sponsored the Beach Boys in Diddle Arena on Friday 3 November 1972. Students had come to hear the music of the sixties and heard little of it; the Talisman reported the concert was not well received until the band turned to its golden oldies, and that many went home disappointed.

Yater wins the presidency; new officers installed

The Herald reported Steve Yater's win in the spring election under 'Associated Student Government Election Returns,' profiling him as making a good impression in his first Congress contact and stressing a calm approach. The same issue covered new officers being installed at a Congress party.

In the recordHerald 52:50, 13 Apr 1973 PDF

28 August 1973

Regents raise the ASG allotment

The Herald opened the year reporting a budget bulge: the Board of Regents voted to increase the Associated Student Government allotment. A companion piece introduced freshmen to ASG under the headline 'Every College Has One.'

In the recordHerald 53:1, 28 Aug 1973 PDF

28 August 1973Other

An $11,000 budget increase pays for the concert and lecture year

The Board of Regents approved an $11,000 increase in the student affairs budget allocated to ASG in place of a proposed head fee rise. President Steve Yater said the increase was better than a higher head fee because it took no additional money from students' pockets, and the Talisman credited it with paying for the Doobie Brothers, Seals and Crofts and the mini-concerts.

$11,000 increase in the ASG allotment

In the record1974 Talisman, Associated Student Government

September 1973Concert

Street dance and Ginger open the year at the amphitheatre

ASG began the year with the traditional street dance during registration week, then followed a few days later with the rock band Ginger in a mini-concert at the outdoor amphitheatre. It was the first outdoor performance at the fine arts amphitheatre and the first of the year's mini-concert series.

In the record1974 Talisman, Entertainment

September 1973Programme

Student-Faculty Interaction seminars

ASG set up a series of informative seminars under a Student-Faculty Interaction Program, run with the undergraduate advisement office. The programmes were informal meetings between students and department representatives to discuss possible majors, aimed at students who had not decided.

In the record1974 Talisman, Associated Student Government

6 September 1973Festival

Stringbean headlines the second Bluegrass Festival

The second Bluegrass Festival was held on 6 September 1973 with the Hee Haw star Stringbean and other Nashville acts. The Herald reported five days later that a country-western 'git-together' had replaced the bluegrass festival.

In the record1974 Talisman, Entertainment

18 September 1973

Free University continues, smaller

ASG's Free University of no-cost, no-credit evening courses continued for another year, though with fewer courses than before.

In the recordHerald 53:6, 18 Sep 1973 PDF

25 September 1973

Housing survey urges dorm improvements

An ASG housing survey urged improvement in dormitory conditions, part of a fall agenda that also included a committee on part-time student opportunities and a push for paper recycling.

In the recordHerald 53:8, 25 Sep 1973 PDF

October 1973Concert

Homecoming rock and roll revival: Jerry Lee Lewis cancels and Chuck Berry never shows

ASG's first attempt at a major concert, a 1950s Rock and Roll Revival for Homecoming, collapsed twice. Jerry Lee Lewis was first booked and cancelled over management problems, Chuck Berry was signed in his place and then took an unscheduled holiday in Las Vegas and ignored the date, leaving Gary U.S. Bonds to headline with the Crystals, Freddie Cannon and Lloyd Price. Ron Beck warned the crowd before the show and offered refunds to anyone who left within fifteen minutes, and he and ASG were still trying to recover the refund money from producer Richard Nader months later.

In the record1974 Talisman, Entertainment

October 1973Tradition

Red Snapper plays the ASG Homecoming dance

The Homecoming dance sponsored by ASG ran from 8pm to midnight after the game against Morehead, with music by Red Snapper. Homecoming 1973 took its theme from the movies and drew a crowd of 19,500 to the game in the rain.

In the record1974 Talisman, Homecoming

13 October 1973Concert

Ethos plays the second mini-concert

The electronic-rock group Ethos from Fort Wayne, Indiana, played ASG's second mini-concert on 13 October 1973 in Van Meter Auditorium. Guitarist Bill Sharpe told the boogie-oriented audience that most of the boogies would have to be in their noses; the band was warmly received and returned in the spring as an off-campus support act.

In the record1974 Talisman, Entertainment

29 October 1973Other

A student takes the concert complaints to Congress

Tony Agee, a junior from Albany, brought his and his friends' grievances before the ASG Congress at the meeting of 29 October 1973. He charged that ASG had misrepresented facts, used false advertising and put incompetent people in charge of booking; president Steve Yater blamed the producer of the Homecoming revival.

In the record1974 Talisman, Entertainment

November 1973Concert

Amnesty is the least successful mini-concert of the series

The soul-blues-jazz combo Amnesty played a mini-concert in Van Meter. The Talisman said much of the crowd enjoyed it but that it was the least successful show of the mini-concert series.

In the record1974 Talisman, Entertainment

4 December 1973

A congressman resigns in protest

ASG representative Reginald Glass resigned his post in protest, the Herald reported, an early sign of strain inside the congress.

In the recordHerald 53:26, 4 Dec 1973 PDF

4 December 1973Concert

The Doobie Brothers play to 6,000

The Doobie Brothers played Diddle Arena on 4 December 1973 before a crowd of 6,000. The group had originally been booked for October and was postponed over a recording commitment; the Herald called the show average but the Talisman said it pleased most of the crowd.

attendance 6,000

In the record1974 Talisman, Entertainment

19 January 1974Concert

Seals and Crofts play the first free concert in more than a year

Seals and Crofts opened the spring semester on Saturday 19 January 1974 before one of the largest crowds ever to see a show in Diddle Arena. The Talisman called it in some ways the best campus concert in more than a year and the first free concert since the autumn of 1972, scheduling and money having prevented one since.

22 January 1974Programme

The Free University shuts down after two semesters

The Herald reported that the Free U had shut down after two semesters. Coordinator Glenn Jackson blamed a lack of student interest and the difficulty of finding people to teach the classes, which had covered knitting, photography, yoga and other subjects.

In the recordCollege Heights Herald 53:32, 22 Jan 1974

February 1974Lecture

Raymond McNally lectures on Dracula

ASG brought Dr Raymond McNally of Boston College, co-author of 'In Search of Dracula', to lecture on vampirism before a large audience in the Garrett Conference Center Ballroom. He traced the legend to a fifteenth century Romanian prince and showed clips from vampire films.

In the record1974 Talisman, Entertainment and Lectures

ASG considers ending the legal loan fund

The Herald reported that ASG might end its legal loan fund. The Legal Rights Committee had been working towards a bail-bond fund for arrested students and had taken up drug expulsions, the refusal to show X-rated films in the student center and the 'Fly' censorship case.

ASG contracted Senator Sam Ervin, chairman of the Senate Watergate committee, to speak at Western on April 2. The same issue reported ASG acting to revamp its committees.

Spending limit stays

ASG voted to retain its campaign spending limit rather than loosen the cap on campaign outlays.

ASG scheduled the folk singer and balladeer Harry Chapin for two shows in Van Meter on 3 March 1974. Activities vice president Tom LaCivita called it the first example of his new concept of major-mini concerts, in which medium-priced performers were brought in, sometimes free and sometimes as a pay event.

Jeff Consolo and Steve Henry won the spring ASG election, in a cycle whose primary the Herald said showed Greek influence. Henry resigned his post over the student discount program after the results.

The Herald reported that Steve Henry had resigned his ASG discount post. Henry was elected ASG president a year later and ran on a platform of entertainment and student services.

Herald calls the lecture series ASG's best effort to date

The Herald judged ASG's 1973-74 lecture series its best effort yet. The series had carried Senator Barry Goldwater, former attorney general Elliot Richardson and Senator Edmund Muskie, and ASG jointly sponsored the psychic Uri Geller with the University Lecture Series.

Marshall Tucker Band is upstaged by Freddie King

ASG brought the Marshall Tucker Band to Diddle Arena on Monday 8 April 1974, with Freddie King leading in. The Talisman said King, brought back for encores by a screaming crowd, was the biggest crowd pleaser, while Diddle's acoustics destroyed much of Marshall Tucker's set and the disappointed crowd began drifting towards the doors halfway through.

Five students filed for the student seat on the Board of Regents ahead of the spring vote, the position that carried a place at the board table.

28 August 1974Festival

Rain drives the Bluegrass Festival indoors

ASG sponsored a Bluegrass Festival on 28 August 1974, headlined by Lester Flatt and the Clinch Mountain Clan, who described their music as folk music with overdrive. Scheduled as an outdoor festival in the amphitheatre, it had to be moved into Van Meter Auditorium because of rain.

September 1974Other

A $42,000 entertainment budget, $27,000 of it for two free concerts

ASG operated on a budget of $42,000 for all forms of entertainment in 1974-75. It set aside $27,000 for two free concerts and $15,000 for mini-concerts, dances and other acts, with major concerts financed by their own gate receipts.

$42,000 entertainment budget; $27,000 for two free concerts, $15,000 for mini-concerts and dances

September 1974Concert

Barefoot Jerry costs ASG almost $1,500

The Nashville group Barefoot Jerry entertained a small crowd in Van Meter with a set that ranged across rock, country, blues and jazz and ended in a standing ovation. Activities vice president Tom LaCivita said ASG lost almost $1,500 on it; the Talisman, which does not date the show, called it one of the finer shows of its size at Western.

lost almost $1,500

A better and cheaper student discount card

ASG changed the student discount card for what the Talisman described as a far better and cheaper one. The change was listed among the accomplishments of the Consolo administration alongside the new academic complaint system.

27 September 1974

Keffer wins freshman vote; Consolo names eight to congress

The Herald reported that Jay Keffer won the freshman election for the top freshman post. In the same issue, ASG president Jeff Consolo tabbed eight students for seats in the ASG congress, and the Academic Council heard a proposal for more student votes.

In the recordHerald 50:9, 27 Sep 1974 PDF

11 October 1974Concert

Students picket the Doc Severinsen Homecoming concert

Doc Severinsen played the Homecoming concert on 11 October 1974 with Today's Children and the Now Generation Brass, before roughly 3,000 people, a substantial majority of them alumni. About thirty students picketed the doors; Severinsen complimented the audience for braving the picket lines and said he respected the demonstrators' right to exercise an American privilege.

attendance about 3,000

15 October 1974

Protesters urge ASG revamping

Protesters urged a revamping of the Associated Student Government. The same issue carried Janet Steen's report that ASG ecology projects were non-existent.

15 October 1974Other

Protest produces a coalition for change in concert booking

The Herald reported that the protest at the Severinsen concert had prompted a coalition seeking change in concert booking. The Student Action Committee that resulted argued that Ron Beck did not have the time the booking job needed and sought power for the activities vice president to negotiate with acts; Kentucky law prevented a student from controlling the funds, so the role stayed advisory, and the committee later folded into ASG's Student Activities Committee.

In the recordCollege Heights Herald, 15 Oct 1974

3 November 1974Concert

Al Stewart's mini-concert dies with his US tour

ASG booked Al Stewart for a mini-concert on 3 November 1974, but his United States tour was cancelled over immigration law. Tom LaCivita booked Kiss in his place, in an effort to ease the pressure students had put on ASG over its choice of acts.

In the record1975 Talisman, Entertainment

7 November 1974Concert

America plays free and pushes ASG further into debt

ASG presented America as the first free concert of the school year on 7 November 1974, with Chad Stewart of Chad and Jeremy opening. Cracked speakers and feedback marred the sound, but lighters brought the band back for 'A Horse with No Name'; the Talisman recorded that ASG went into steadily increasing debt by presenting America free.

19 November 1974

ASG schedules Kiss and initiates concert hour

ASG scheduled the rock band Kiss and initiated a concert hour, part of its role booking campus entertainment that fall. The concert program later became a major source of financial trouble for the organization.

6 December 1974Service

ASG establishes a service area

Jim Reynolds reported in the Herald that ASG had established a service area. The reorganisation of that year had put ASG's work into two areas, student affairs and academic affairs, with projects assigned to one or the other.

In the recordCollege Heights Herald, 6 Dec 1974

7 December 1974Concert

Kiss plays Van Meter and Ron Beck swears off the genre

Kiss played to a capacity crowd in Van Meter Auditorium on 7 December 1974, with smoke bombs, fire-eating, whiteface and leather bat wings, and Gene Simmons simulating vomiting and dripping stage blood over the front row. Ron Beck said afterwards that he would never again take part in booking this kind of act for Western because the show had no educational value for students.

21 January 1975

ASG rescues the Student Volunteer Bureau

ASG agreed to administer the Student Volunteer Bureau. The Herald reported that the bureau was rescued by the student government's action.

21 January 1975Service

Volunteer Bureau and tutorial programme absorbed into ASG

The Student Volunteer Bureau, which placed students in community volunteer work, was weakened when founder Rodney Berry could not secure administrators or funds. Berry approached president Jeff Consolo about folding it into ASG, and the merger passed at the last meeting of the fall semester by better than 80 per cent; the tutorial programme was consolidated into ASG at the same time.

ASG action was halted twice during the week by a lack of quorum. A Herald editorial said the confusion in ASG signaled a need for change.

ASG's first major spring concert put War and the Charlie Daniels Band in Diddle Arena on 3 March 1975. Students called the Charlie Daniels set the best they had had in years and matches and lighters brought him back for 'Orange Blossom Special', but attendance was very low.

26 August 1975Other

Regents add $16,000 to the entertainment budget and buy a second free concert

The Board of Regents passed a $16,000 increase in the ASG entertainment budget in August 1975. President Steve Henry said the increase allowed a second free concert and that he had never known one year to have two free concerts, much less two in a semester.

$16,000 increase in the ASG entertainment budget

In the recordCollege Heights Herald 51:1, 26 Aug 1975

September 1975Concert

Gove, Alex Harvey and Bottom and Company welcome students back

Two free concerts opened the fall semester to welcome students back, featuring Gove, Alex Harvey and Bottom and Company at the fine arts centre outdoor theatre. Harvey picked a dulcimer with a feather during his set.

In the record1976 Talisman, Concerts

11 September 1975Concert

ASG sponsors LAMB, a messianic music duo

On 11 September 1975 ASG sponsored LAMB, a duo specialising in messianic music, in Van Meter Auditorium. The Talisman noted the concert was well attended, perhaps because many students had writing assignments for MC 272 classes that required it.

In the record1976 Talisman, Concerts

17 September 1975Concert

Loggins and Messina open the season and lose $7,000

Kenny Loggins and Jim Messina played the first major concert of the year in Diddle Arena on Wednesday 17 September 1975, with the Amazing Rhythm Aces also on the bill. The crowd of 4,300 was too small and ASG lost about $7,000; activities vice president Rick Kelley blamed a lack of student body support.

lost about $7,000; attendance 4,300

19 September 1975

Big concert, big loss

An ASG concert drew 4,300 people but lost $7,000, the Herald reported, opening a money argument that ran through the fall.

23 September 1975Lecture

Jules Bergman speaks on '2000 A.D. - The Way it Will Be'

ABC science editor Jules Bergman came to campus on 23 September 1975 for the first guest of the University Lecture Series, which the Talisman notes was also sponsored by ASG. Poor weather hurt the crowd; Bergman said man was adaptable enough to fly to the moon six times but could not endure much longer what he had created for himself on earth.

30 October 1975Concert

Doug Kershaw takes three encores in Homecoming week

ASG brought the Cajun fiddler Doug Kershaw for the Thursday night of Homecoming week, 30 October 1975. About 700 people saw him jump into the crowd to lead 'Jambalaya' and land in the lap of a startled coed in the fourth row; he took three encores and closed with 'Louisiana Man'.

attendance about 700

31 October 1975Lecture

Pat Paulsen returns for a free 'Lecture in Humor'

Pat Paulsen entertained a Diddle Arena crowd on Homecoming eve, 31 October 1975, at a free show sponsored by ASG. Presenting 'A Lecture in Humor', he traced the history of comedy from prehistoric times to the future and said he had found out you cannot speak your mind and expect to get elected.

25 November 1975

A budget remedy and a book exchange

The Herald weighed whether a new ASG budget offered a remedy, and reported a spring semester book exchange to be co-sponsored by ASG and Veterans on Campus. President Steve Henry moved to change the concert proposal the same week.

2 December 1975Other

ASG creates a student activities committee for concerts, lectures and publicity

To settle the dispute over booking, ASG adopted a Student Activities Committee, put into operation on 2 December 1975 and chaired by Rick Kelley. From 63 applicants, 17 members were chosen across three subcommittees, seven for concerts, five for lectures and five for publicity, each with alternates.

12 January 1976Service

ASG and Veterans on Campus run a book exchange against the bookstore

To give students an alternative to the College Heights Bookstore, ASG co-sponsored a book exchange with Veterans on Campus from 12 to 26 January 1976. Administrative vice president Christy Vogt said the two groups had covered expenses by 21 January through the sale of over 600 books, with ASG and VOC making 25 cents on each book sold.

over 600 books sold; 25 cents profit per book

26 January 1976Service

A second campus check-cashing facility opens after an ASG survey

An ASG survey at fall registration found that the most significant desire of students was a new check-cashing facility. A second campus check-cashing point opened in the customer service area of the bookstore on 26 January 1976 for nine hours a week, after the original proposal for a full-service campus bank branch was judged impractical by area bankers.

In the record1976 Talisman, ASG

30 January 1976Concert

The Spinners and Wet Willie draw 7,500 to a free concert

The free concert by the Spinners and Wet Willie on 30 January 1976 attracted 7,500 people, the second straight major ASG promotion to make money. The Spinners impersonated the Ink Spots, the Mills Brothers, Tom Jones, the Miracles and Elvis Presley and donned wigs for the Supremes; it was the first concert the new Student Activities Committee helped bring about.

attendance 7,500

6 February 1976Lecture

George Wallace is fought over in committee and never appears

President Steve Henry reported a 99 per cent chance of getting George Wallace, then seeking the Democratic presidential nomination, to speak in April 1976. A subcommittee of ASG's Student Activities Committee voted 4-2 with one abstention on 6 February to strike Wallace from the list of lecturers on the grounds that the arrangements had been made improperly, ASG Congress overruled the resolution, and by 13 February the Herald reported the lecture was uncertain; no appearance is recorded.

In the recordCollege Heights Herald 51:38, 6 Feb 1976

12 February 1976Lecture

George Allen lectures on success and ambition

George Allen, head coach of the Washington Redskins, spoke in the Garrett Conference Center on 12 February 1976 in one of the spring ASG-sponsored lectures. He showed a film, answered questions on professional football and advised those facing a tight job market that the last thing to talk about when looking for a job is money.

In the recordCollege Heights Herald 51:40, 13 Feb 1976

Chris Miller of National Lampoon draws 1,100 and a rebuke from the dean

Chris Miller of National Lampoon drew about 1,100 people to the Garrett Conference Center on 24 February 1976 with a lecture titled 'Toe Sucking in Albania, or An Evening of Erotic Laughter'. Three days later the Herald reported that dean of student affairs Charles Keown had criticised ASG's taste in sponsoring the lecture.

attendance about 1,100

Faulk impeachment hearings open as campaign begins

The Associated Student Government began impeachment hearings against congress member Gerard Faulk the same week candidates for the spring election, including Christy Vogt, were set to speak to students. An editorial the same issue held up Associated Student Government's troubles as a cautionary example for the university's newly forming Faculty Senate.

Laundry improvements take effect

From 15 April 1976 the university installed more washers and dryers, an air-conditioned study area and a laundry pick-up service, with dry cleaning by a local firm in the proposal. Steve Henry said he hoped the facilities, which ASG had proposed the previous October, would be long-lasting.

27 April 1976

Herald supplement recaps a year of ASG wins

A special supplement to the Herald, paid for and written by the Associated Student Government, summed up the outgoing Henry administration's year: women's hours abolished with ASG's backing, better intramural facilities credited to ASG resolutions, a new ASG discount card program, a second campus site for cashing checks, and a Veterans on Campus book exchange. The supplement also printed the year's roster of congress members and its bills and resolutions, and carried Christy Vogt's own piece on laundry facility improvement.

27 April 1976Service

ASG's own supplement counts the discount cards and the book exchange

In the Student Insight supplement it paid for and wrote itself, ASG set out its services for the year: the discount cards it sponsored, the book exchange run with Veterans on Campus which it called a success, and its work on laundry facilities and intramural facilities. Christy Vogt wrote the piece on laundry improvements and Elaine Boeckman the piece on the abolition of women's hours.

ASG creates constitutional revision committee

The Associated Student Government congress passed Bill 2, creating a committee charged with revising the organization's constitution. Constitutional revision remained on the ASG agenda for the rest of the school year and appeared again among proposed amendments and a spring referendum bill.

Bob Woodward cancels and comes six months late

Carl Bernstein was booked to open the lecture season but contracted pneumonia, and his partner Bob Woodward was announced as a substitute before cancelling his Western and University of Kentucky dates for work. Promoters paid the advertising costs for the cancelled lecture, but someone in the ASG office drew a bull's-eye on Woodward's publicity poster; he finally appeared in early April 1977.

15 October 1976Concert

Chicago grosses $53,092 and becomes Western's most successful concert

Chicago appeared at Diddle Arena on 15 October 1976, drew 10,450 people and grossed $53,092, the most financially successful concert Western had staged. The show cost $25,000 and was promoted by Reggae Ltd of St Louis with ASG, the first privately promoted concert at Western; about 5,000 advance tickets were sold, another record, and Ron Beck called it one of the best the university had ever had.

The congress adopted Resolution 13, proposing that Western institute a minimum wage policy for all student employees. It was part of a heavy fall docket that also included resolutions on parking, laundry services, non-smoking areas and residence hall change machines.

Members of the ASG lecture committee, David Carwell, Ricky Sheppard and Mike Seiler, hosted the visiting speakers.

29 April 1978Other

$23,000 of losses nearly cost ASG the concert programme

After ASG lost more than $23,000 on major concerts across the year, dean of student affairs Charles Keown recommended to the Board of Regents that its entertainment budget be halved for 1978-79 and that a committee study whether the University Center Board should take over programming. Bob Moore argued at the 29 April meeting that students would have less involvement if the change were made, and the regents voted to let ASG keep its full $62,000 entertainment budget while directing President Downing to appoint the study committee.

1978Concert

John Prine sells out Van Meter and ASG still loses $2,000

John Prine came to Western in the autumn of 1978 and did what no other musical act had done in a long time, playing to a capacity house. But Van Meter Auditorium holds only slightly more than 1,000, and even with a sellout and tickets priced higher than any previous mini-concert, ASG lost about $2,000 on the show. His five-man band ran through 25 songs, among them "Spanish Pipedream," "Dear Abby," "The Bottomless Lake" and "Sam Stone."

The Board of Regents gave ASG authority to seek outside help booking concerts, and ASG contracted Sunshine Promotions of Indianapolis, producers of a Rolling Stones show in Lexington that summer and of Summer Jam II in Louisville. The firm had booked more than 150 concerts; for its part of the bargain ASG was to receive 13 percent of the net profits. Player and Exile play the Homecoming concert

Player and Exile played Diddle Arena on Homecoming night to 4,296 people. Player, whose hits were "This Time I'm In It For Love" and "Baby Come Back," failed to get the crowd on its feet; Exile, from Richmond, skipped its sound check and played through poor sound but had the arena standing. After $24,000 in production costs and Western's 13 percent cut of a $25,694.29 after-tax gross, the Talisman recorded that there was little financial success to speak of.

9 November 1978Programme

The Herald tells ASG to quit the concert business

An unsigned Herald editorial said it was time ASG got out of the concert business, arguing that concert promotion had taken most of the organisation's time and effort and that ASG could not even hire a promoter competently. It cited excessive university demands, poor communication with Sunshine Promotions and the unsigned contract behind the Homecoming show. The same issue carried a reader's letter defending the concert as good.

In the recordCollege Heights Herald, Vol. 54, No. 23, 9 November 1978

28 November 1978Concert

Joe Cocker drops out; Wet Willie takes his place

Joe Cocker, who had been announced to appear with the Outlaws at Diddle Arena on 5 December, cancelled his entire tour, and Sunshine Promotions signed the southern rock band Wet Willie in his place. Advertisements in that issue read "ASG and WKU Present" the Outlaws with special guest Wet Willie, 7:30 p.m., $6 in advance and $7 on the day of the show. The same meeting heard that Eleanor Smeal, president of the National Organization for Women, would speak on 7 December in Van Meter Auditorium.

$6 advance, $7 day of show

In the recordCollege Heights Herald, Vol. 54, No. 27, 28 November 1978

30 November 1978

ASG approves revised constitution

The congress approved a revised Associated Student Government constitution. The revision capped a fall in which ASG also pushed teacher evaluations and parking rezoning.

In the recordHerald 54:28, 30 Nov 1978 PDF

5 December 1978Concert

The Outlaws cancel after 242 tickets sell

Reaction to the advertising for the Outlaws and Wet Willie was so poor that only 242 tickets had been sold by the week of the show. When the Outlaws' manager heard the figure he cancelled on the spot, according to university programs coordinator Tim Nemeth. The December date, ASG's replacement for the Joe Cocker booking, never happened.

242 tickets sold

8 January 1979campus

John Minton sworn in as interim president

Vice President John Minton was sworn in as WKU's interim president by Judge Charles Reynolds, succeeding Dero Downing and holding the post until Donald Zacharias took office that August.

In the recordWKU Timeline: John Minton

The Associated Student Government signed three lectures for the spring semester, part of its ongoing role booking campus speakers.

18 January 1979Lecture

Eleanor Smeal's lecture keeps slipping

Activities vice president David Carwell told ASG's first meeting of the semester that the university was still trying to reschedule a lecture by Eleanor Smeal, president of the National Organization for Women, for February or March; she had been announced for 7 December and had not come. He set out what ASG was paying the three speakers it had signed: $4,000 for Dick Gregory, $2,000 for Princeton professor Gerard O'Neill and $2,000 for Congresswoman Shirley Chisholm, plus expenses, with all the lectures free. Carwell added that tickets for the Heart concert at Diddle Arena on 15 February would go on sale on 22 January at $7 in advance and $8 on the day.

Gregory $4,000; O'Neill $2,000; Chisholm $2,000; Heart tickets $7 advance, $8 day of show

15 February 1979Concert

Heart at Diddle Arena

Heart played Diddle Arena on 15 February with Ann Wilson opening on "High Times" and her sister Nancy on guitar, running through "Heartless," "Straight On," "Magazine," "Mistral Wind," "Dog and Butterfly," "Hijinx," "Crazy on You" and "Barracuda." Sunshine Promotions had signed the band as its first major break for Western, but only 5,821 came, a little more than half of capacity. Western made about $5,200 from the show, the one clear financial success of the concert year.

Western made about $5,200; 5,821 attended

Thornton and Craig win seats on Kentucky's student government council

27 March 1979Programme

Forum '79 cut to one night

ASG's gubernatorial candidates' discussion panel, scheduled for two nights, was shortened to one after the university orchestra needed Van Meter Auditorium on the Monday. President Steve Thornton said the surviving session would run at 7:30 p.m. on the Tuesday, with Democrats Carroll Hubbard, Ralph Ed Graves and George Atkins appearing and Lieutenant Governor Thelma Stovall sending a representative. Ray White was the only Republican candidate willing to attend; Terry McBrayer and Louie Nunn stayed away.

In the recordCollege Heights Herald, Vol. 54, No. 48, 27 March 1979

31 March 1979Programme

Regents take concerts and lectures away from ASG

On 31 March the Board of Regents approved moving the activities that ASG had run, lectures and concerts among them, to a rebuilt University Center Board and funded that board with $80,000 for programming from autumn 1979. The new committees were to include the ASG president, the activities vice president and one congress member alongside Greek, United Black Students, residence hall and faculty representatives. Programs coordinator Tim Nemeth said the new board would involve at most ten students in lectures and concerts where ASG had involved fifty.

$80,000 to the University Center Board

1981-82

Marcell Bush (president) · David Payne (president)

17 entries · 55 index lines

3 September 1981

ASG announces its goals for the year

The Associated Student Government announced its goals for the coming year. Within two weeks its executives were defending their actions in the Herald, whose editorial page complained that petty politics plagued the organization.

In the recordHerald 57:4, 3 Sep 1981 PDF

10 September 1981Service

The discount cards that never existed

ASG announced it would file complaints with the Better Business Bureaus of Georgia and Texas against University Press Inc. of Lewisville, Texas, and Atlanta, which had taken $275 from each of at least four Bowling Green merchants for ASG-endorsed student discount cards that were never produced. A man calling himself Louis F. Cordoba had told Gary Smith of the Bouquet Shoppe on the U.S. 31-W By-Pass that then-president Steve Fuller had recommended his shop as an advertiser, and Smith wrote a $275 cheque on 18 March. The cards were supposed to have been handed out at registration for the autumn.

$275 taken from each of at least four merchants

In the recordCollege Heights Herald, Vol. 57, No. 5, 10 September 1981

24 September 1981

Campaign spending limit raised

ASG voted to increase its campaign spending limit. The change followed a week of debate over whether the cap should rise.

In the recordHerald 57:9, 24 Sep 1981 PDF

29 September 1981Service

14,000 cards, a dead phone line and a returned letter

President Marcel Bush had spent three weeks trying to reach the company printing 14,000 ASG discount cards: the Texas number was disconnected, an answering service pushed her to an Atlanta number nobody answered, and a letter to the Texas address came back from the post office. On the day complaints were being filed, company representative Phil Bewley finally telephoned to say the cards had shipped from New York and that printing problems had caused the delay. The Herald noted that until two years earlier ASG had printed discount cards at its own expense as a free student service, charging merchants nothing, and had dropped it when costs became prohibitive.

14,000 cards; merchants paid $275 for a listing

In the recordCollege Heights Herald, Vol. 57, No. 10, 29 September 1981

ASG vetoes plan to pay an education lobbyist

The Associated Student Government vetoed a plan to pay an education lobbyist. The vote came weeks after ASG had rallied publicly for higher education funding.

The Herald reported that the Associated Student Government had appointed a council to decide disputes inside the organization. The story ran two weeks after the same reporter, Kevin Francke, covered the resignation of ASG president Marcel Bush.

2 September 1982Service

A volunteer student escort service

A student escort service jointly sponsored by Interhall Council, ASG and the university police began operating, walking women anywhere on campus from dark until midnight Sunday to Thursday on a single telephone number, with a vehicle in bad weather. Coordinator James Hunter said Western was the first university in the country with a completely volunteer, student-operated escort service, and that it had filled about 500 to 600 requests in its first year without a single incident. Public safety director Paul Bunch said requests for escorts had tripled after two students were raped the previous year.

500 to 600 requests filled in the first year

In the recordCollege Heights Herald, Vol. 58, No. 4, 2 September 1982

18 November 1982

ASG approves a coed housing bill

Monica Dias reported that the Associated Student Government had approved a coed housing bill. The measure built through the fall: ASG and the Interhall Council polled students on coed housing in September, and ASG formally proposed it on 10 November.

In the recordHerald 58:25, 18 Nov 1982 PDF

12 April 1983

ASG election day: candidates court votes for the top offices

The Herald urged students to the polls for the Associated Student Government election. Beyond the presidential contest, candidates for ASG's other top offices - including Bob Shults, Laura McClellan, Traci Turner, Kim Binkley and Allan Kujala - each drew endorsement letters in the paper; the Herald index does not specify which office each sought.

In the recordHerald 58:54, 12 Apr 1983 PDF

Escort service returns; discount card floated

The Herald's opening issue reported that the student escort service would resume and that ASG might sponsor a discount card. Filing for freshman elections was set to begin September 19.

30 August 1983

Smith opens with a "year of action"

Steve Paul reported that the Associated Student Government was planning for a year of action. The story ran in the third issue of the fall semester, a week after the Herald first reported that ASG might sponsor a discount card.

In the recordHerald 59:3, 30 Aug 1983 PDF

September 1983

Discount card plan draws fire

ASG voted to study the discount card after the Herald editorialized that the organization should govern, not market cards. A week later the paper reported ASG would offer members a commission on card sales, prompting letters calling the plan cheap shots and old tricks.

ASG takes up a university day-care center

10 November 1983Service

ASG prints the discount card itself

After an agreement collapsed with University Services Associates of St. Mary's, Missouri, ASG voted to print the student discount cards itself, and they were finally handed out in November through the Student Affairs and Public Relations committees working with Interhall Council. Nine businesses appeared on the card, among them the seven merchants who had paid company president George Wheaton for the original card and never got a refund. President Jack Smith said the businesses would have to recover their own money: "They got what they paid for. They got their discount card."

nine businesses on the card; seven merchants unrefunded

1984-85

Jack Smith (president)

18 entries · 50 index lines

20 September 1984

Four proposals made reality in the third week of class

The Herald reported that four Associated Student Government proposals had already been carried out, and that the congress was beginning a study of a student book exchange. The exchange went on to become the running project of the year.

In the recordHerald 60:7, 20 Sep 1984 PDF

20 September 1984Service

ASG votes to study a book exchange

ASG voted to study the feasibility of a student book exchange and formed a committee to examine schemes at the universities of Louisville and Kentucky. Two models were discussed: a room where students sold and bought books at prices they set, and a cheaper list of students, telephone numbers, books for sale and asking prices. President Jack Smith said books were more expensive every year and students needed somewhere besides the College Heights Bookstore, adding, "I don't think there's anything wrong with a little competition."

In the recordCollege Heights Herald, Vol. 60, No. 7, 20 September 1984

27 September 1984

The grade scale proposal is denied

ASG's proposal for a new grade scale was denied, one week after the congress's early run of successes. It was the first setback of the fall reported in the Herald's coverage.

In the recordHerald 60:9, 27 Sep 1984 PDF

18 October 1984

ASG wants less general education

The congress went on record wanting a reduction in general education requirements. It was an early instance of the body intervening in curriculum policy, three years before the fights over the General Education Task Force.

In the recordHerald 60:15, 18 Oct 1984 PDF

8 November 1984

LaMont Jones drops out of a revote

LaMont Jones withdrew from an ASG revote, and the same issue carried an editorial cartoon on the organization. A disputed election requiring a revote marked the low point of the fall semester.

In the recordHerald 60:19, 8 Nov 1984 PDF

29 November 1984Service

Book exchange ambassadors work the campus

ASG sent "ambassadors" out to campus organisations to explain the new book exchange and hand out registration cards, with public relations vice president John Holland promising to send a speaker "faster than Domino's pizza." Registration cards went into campus mailboxes on 5 December and had to be returned by 21 December, with an off-campus coupon printed in the Herald. The list of available books was to be compiled over Christmas and published as a tabloid of names, telephone numbers and titles when students returned in January.

In the recordCollege Heights Herald, Vol. 60, No. 24, 29 November 1984

1985Service

The book exchanger's first edition

The tabloid book exchanger was distributed in the first week of the spring semester and students began telephoning each other to haggle over used textbooks. Committee co-chairmen John Holland and senior class president Danny Broderick, with President Jack Smith and administrative secretary Debra Stahl, keyed the entries into an IBM Personal Computer over the Christmas break on a program written for $25 by Bill Chestnut, a computer science graduate from Berea; Ginger Williams of the Franklin Favorite did the typesetting. Smith said the University of Kentucky had listed 700 books in its first exchange and Western had double that, and Broderick said ASG made no money from it: "This was a labor of love."

$25 paid for the computer program; about 1,400 books listed

In the recordTalisman 1985 ("What Did You Expect?")

5 March 1985Tradition

ASG takes Big Brothers/Big Sisters children to a Lady Toppers game

Congress members each paired themselves with a child from Big Brothers/Big Sisters of Bowling Green for the women's last home basketball game, spending the evening counting heads, running trips to the bathroom and making enough noise to see the Lady Toppers past Cincinnati 122-72. Before the game the children ate snacks, made banners for the spirit contest and played pool and video games in the university center. The Herald reported that mothers in the crowd gave the student government members understanding looks.

In the recordCollege Heights Herald, Vol. 60, No. 43, 5 March 1985

10 October 1985Service

The commonwealth attorney is asked to find the discount card printer

ASG's student discount cards finally went out in October after Phil Bewley of Parkland Publishers Inc. missed two August deadlines and the Warren County Commonwealth Attorney's Office was called in to find him. Bewley, reached by telephone in Nashville, said he believed President Mitchell McKinney had understood the cards would not be ready until 23 September, and blamed printer trouble. It was the second time in five years the same representative had left an ASG discount card in limbo.

In the recordCollege Heights Herald, Vol. 61, No. 13, 10 October 1985

About 20 votes separated the top two finishers in a fall ASG election, and the congress debated setting a grade-point average requirement for its own members. Both stories ran in the same late-October issue.

November 1985Tradition

ASG wins its division of November Nonsense

ASG was the only non-Greek group to enter November Nonsense, the variety show Chi Omega has staged since 1965, and took first place in the organisation division. Its skit followed an orange-faced, loud-mouthed "oompah" projected from 1965, when he was a star Western footballer, to 1985, when he became a potential candidate for the university presidency. Seven groups performed four-to-six minute skits on a "Back to the Future" theme, and the sorority raised about $800 for Hospice.

about $800 raised for Hospice

ASG hosts the state student government conference

ASG hosted the state Student Government Conference at Glasgow to promote involvement and the role of student government. 28 August 1986Service

ASG takes over the student discount card

Associated Student Government took production of the wallet-sized student discount card in house after the company contracted the previous year delayed distribution. The printer, John Bewley, had been indicted by a Warren County grand jury for theft of service over $100 for failing to pay ASG the $500 it was owed for distributing the cards, then paid and had the case dismissed. Administrative vice president Lori Scott said about 20 merchants had already bought advertising at $100 each and she hoped for 30 to 40, with the cards out by the first week of October.

$100 per merchant advertisement, about 20 sold; a $500 debt recovered from the previous printer

1987Programme

Weekend in the Woods, the fourth annual ASG leadership camp

ASG sponsored the fourth annual Weekend in the Woods, a leadership conference at Camp Decker about 13 miles from Bowling Green, and 45 students attended against accommodation for 75 at $30 a head covering meals and lodging. Members had begun lining up speakers and camp reservations the previous March; seminars covered leadership, goal setting, generating ideas and listening, and for the first time student leaders spoke alongside faculty. State senator-elect Nick Kafoglis lectured, and when President Kern Alexander could not make the closing session he invited every Weekender to breakfast at his home a week later. The yearbook does not date the weekend.

$30 per participant, all inclusive

In the record1987 Talisman, 'Branching Out - Weekend in the Woods'

1987Programme

$10,000 for campus lights and a plan for a student hangout

The 1987 Talisman recorded ASG's two main projects of the year as more campus lighting and a student hangout in Downing University Center, both traced to President Kern Alexander's concern about student retention raised at a September breakfast with ASG members. ASG persuaded the administration to put up $10,000 for new lights. To stop students going home at weekends, members formed committees to arrange the music and the lighting for a place in the university center where students could dance without leaving campus.

$10,000 from the administration for new campus lighting

In the record1987 Talisman, 'Governing Bodies'

3 February 1987Service

A recorded campus events phone line is put on hold

A proposal to start a telephone service playing recorded messages about campus events was tabled at the 3 February meeting until more research could be done. The equipment would have cost $500, with $60 for installation and a $17 monthly service charge, and author Bill Schilling said promotion would add $200 more. Public Information director Fred Hensley had not been consulted before the bill was introduced, and the sports information office already ran a line of its own.

$500 equipment, $60 installation, $17 a month, plus $200 promotion

17 November 1987Service

The Book Exchanger gets a third semester and a warning

ASG ran the Book Exchanger for a third semester, a free listing publication in which students advertised used textbooks to each other as an alternative to selling back to the bookstore. Cards went into student mailboxes on 11 November with a 20 November deadline, and about 60 students listed books each semester. Student Affairs chairman Victor Click said the project raised about $60 the previous fall and nothing in the spring against printing costs of about $653, that the year's budget allotted $750 to it, and that he would recommend dropping it if this run failed.

$750 budgeted; about $653 spent on printing the previous year; about $60 raised

In the recordHerald 63:24, 17 Nov 1987

9 February 1988Tradition

The Angie Norcia Award is created for the yearly banquet

At the 9 February meeting student government created an award to present at its yearly banquet in May, named for Angie Norcia, an Owensboro senior who had died the previous summer of adult respiratory distress syndrome and Guillain-Barre syndrome and who had been active in student government for more than two years. President Tim Todd said it would be one of the highest honours given to a congress member, with recipients nominated and interviewed by a committee of members. It survived as the Mary Angela Norcia Memorial Award, still on the banquet nomination list in 1994.

16 February 1988Programme

ASG backs the Frankfort rally for higher education

ASG suspended its rules on 9 February to adopt the standard resolution urging Governor Wallace Wilkinson and the legislature to fund higher education, and presented it at the Frankfort rally on 16 February; Western's was the last of the eight state student governments to pass it. About 3,000 students, faculty and alumni marched up Capitol Avenue in what the Kentucky Advocates for Higher Education called the largest Frankfort demonstration since 1964. Western sent four free buses and 130 of the 161 people who signed up made the trip, joining a Western contingent of about 250, with cheerleaders handing out 250 red towels. A Herald editorial the same week said ASG had choked by passing only a form resolution while Murray State's government ran a write-a-thon that got more than 500 students to write the governor.

In the recordHerald 63:41, 18 Feb 1988

23 February 1988

ASG explains its empty seats

The organization publicly cited its reasons for the vacancies in its ranks, and four congress positions had been filled at a single meeting earlier that month. Days later an editorial told the body it needed better ideas, not gimmicks.

Ragland and Whitehouse win the primaries

Shannon Ragland and Scott Whitehouse won the ASG presidential primaries, narrowing a field of seven. The same issue reported passage of a proposal requesting a memorial area on campus.

29 November 1990

ASG passes resolution for left-handed desks

The Associated Student Government passed Resolution 90-10-F, requesting that a left-handed desk be provided in each classroom. The Herald reported the vote in its 29 November 1990 issue, alongside news that a companion resolution on excused absences had been killed the same week.

29 November 1990

ASG kills resolution on earthquake-prediction absences

The Associated Student Government killed Resolution 90-12-F, which had asked that student absences tied to Iben Browning's widely publicized forecast of a major New Madrid Fault earthquake be excused. Browning had predicted the quake for on or near 3 December 1990; it prompted regional anxiety and some school closures, but no earthquake occurred. The Herald reported the resolution's defeat in its 29 November 1990 issue.

In the recordSGA Legislation, Resolution 90-12-F, "Excused Absences for Earthquake Prediction"

1991

ASG overhauls its by-laws, including veto-override procedure

Herald previews four ASG candidates

Falmlen won the Associated Student Government presidential election in results the Herald reported under the headline "Heather Falmlen Wins Amid Associated Student Government Election Protests." In the recordHerald 67:13, 10 Oct 1991, "Associated Student Government Elections Tuesday"

25 October 1991Festival

International Day, co-sponsored with the University Center Board

More than 800 high school students from around the state came to Western on Friday 25 October for the annual International Day, sponsored by the University Center Board, Associated Student Government, International Programs and Student Affairs. A bazaar on the third floor of Downing University Center sold handmade goods from other countries, including bracelets, ornaments, scarves and belts made by Indian tribes in Ecuador and African woodwork and silver and copper jewellery. Profits from the crafts went to Escuela Para Padres, a joint fundraising organisation working to prevent abuse of women and children; project coordinator Joan Martin said jewellery was the best seller.

In the recordHerald 67:18, 29 Oct 1991

29 October 1991

ASG asks that Iracane not be re-elected regents chair

The Associated Student Government passed Resolution 91-6-F, authored by Mark Miller and Eric McWilliams and sponsored by Mistianna Holcomb, asking that Joe Iracane not be re-elected chair of the Board of Regents. The resolution's text stated that Iracane, chairman for eight consecutive years, was under investigation by the FBI, the IRS and U.S. attorneys in Indiana and Kentucky over an alleged $6 million payment to Pyramid Mining Co. in return for contracts and a separate alleged $14,500 payment to the company for a consulting contract; it also accused him of overstepping into day-to-day university operations reserved for the president under the Board's bylaws. The resolution asked student regent Heather Falmlen to vote against him. No source found reports the investigation's outcome. The same day's Herald covered the vote under "Associated Student Government Opposes Joseph Iracane."

In the recordSGA Resolution 91-6-F, "Board of Regents Chair Term Limit"

31 October 1991

ASG asks the regents to elect a new leader

ASG urged the Board of Regents to elect a new leader in place of chairman Joseph Iracane, two days after the Herald reported the organization's opposition to him. It was a rare direct challenge to the university's governing board.

In the recordHerald 67:19, 31 Oct 1991

5 November 1991Programme

Voter registration drive signs up nearly 1,000 students

ASG ran a voter registration drive for the 5 November 1991 election, led by vice president John Seiber, who with other congress members registered nearly 1,000 Western students. A full-page ASG advertisement in the Herald the following February listed the drive alongside fall break, campus recycling, organizational aid, new picnic tables, a new copier for the science library and the radio show as the year's work, with forums on the election, student concerns, the class presidents and a question and answer session with the regents.

In the recordHerald 67:38, 13 Feb 1992 (ASG advertisement)

6 November 1991

Regents re-elect Iracane despite ASG's resolution

A week after the Associated Student Government asked the Board of Regents not to re-elect Joe Iracane as chair, the board did so anyway. The university's own newsletter reported the result under "Joe Iracane Re-elected to Chair Regents."

In the recordOn Campus 1:16, 6 Nov 1991, "Joe Iracane Re-elected to Chair Regents" PDF

The Residence Hall Association and ASG sent a joint mailing asking parents to support the campus health service. It closed out the health-focused fall Falmlen had promised in August.

In the recordHerald 67:29, 12 Dec 1991

28 January 1992

ASG introduces a bill for a student regent advisory committee

The Associated Student Government introduced Bill #92-01-S, authored by Greg Butler, Mistianna Holcomb, Melony Jones and Melissa Maggard and sponsored by the Public Relations committee, proposing a Student Advisory Committee - made up of the class presidents, a representative from each college and the executive council as ex-officio members - to brief the student regent on Board of Regents agenda items and canvass student opinion before each meeting, two days before the Herald reported the plan.

In the recordSGA Legislation, Bill #92-01-S, "Development of Advisory Committee for Student Regent"

30 January 1992

ASG plans a committee on student access to the regent

The Herald reported the Associated Student Government was planning a committee aimed at securing student access to WKU's regent, amid a statewide debate over how regents were selected.

In the recordHerald 67:34, 30 Jan 1992, "Associated Student Government Plans Regent Committee"

30 January 1992

Editorial cartoon targets Falmlen

The same Herald issue ran an editorial cartoon, "Ventriloquist's Dummy" by Patrick Richardson, with Falmlen as its subject.

In the recordHerald 67:34, 30 Jan 1992, "Editorial Cartoon Heather Falmlen Ventriloquist's Dummy"

24 March 1992Service

A permanent voter registration booth at class registration

Bill 92-06-S, introduced on 24 March 1992 by Trent Lyda for the Legislative Research Committee, committed ASG to keeping a voter registration booth wherever class registration took place each fall and spring, to capitalise on the influx of unregistered eligible student voters. The committee was to coordinate the scheduling of students and organisations willing to staff it, and every ASG member was asked to work the booth for at least an hour during the registration period.

In the recordSGA Records, Bill 92-06-S, Establishment of Permanent Voter Registration Program

2 April 1992

ASG resolves to support football despite budget cuts

The Associated Student Government passed Resolution 92-7-S, declaring its support for the WKU football program in spite of budget cuts. The resolution's own text argued the university had already awarded 67 football scholarships it would be contractually bound to honor even if the program were suspended, calling a suspension that still paid non-playing scholarship athletes an unnecessary expense. This entry corrects the resolution's date: an earlier record in this archive gave 4 February 1992, but the resolution itself is dated introduced 2 April 1992, shortly before the Board of Regents' 1 May vote to keep the program.

In the recordSGA Legislation, Resolution 92-7-S, "Support of Football Program"

7 April 1992

Associated Students votes to become the Student Government Association

The body voted to rename itself on 7 April and students ratified the change in a referendum on 14 April. It took effect that autumn.

In the recordWKU SGA history

7 April 1992

The primary is canceled

The ASG primary election was canceled, with too few candidates to require one, and a parking bill sat in committee the same week. The general election went ahead the following Tuesday.

In the recordHerald 67:50, 7 Apr 1992

16 April 1992

Joe Rains wins big as 1,200 turn out

Joe Rains won the presidential election by a wide margin, with about 1,200 students casting votes. The same ballot carried the constitutional amendments students had voted on two days earlier, including the name change.

In the recordHerald 67:53, 16 Apr 1992

21 April 1992

Rains to oversee the change to SGA

The Herald reported that incoming president Joe Rains would oversee the transition from the Associated Student Government to the Student Government Association. Student reaction to the spring's parking bill was reported as varied in the same issue.

In the recordHerald 67:54, 21 Apr 1992

21 April 1992

Rains takes office with a rename to carry out

The Herald reported that incoming president Joe Rains would oversee the change from Associated Student Government to Student Government Association, which students had ratified by referendum the week before. The new name took effect that fall, making Rains the first president to serve under it.

In the recordHerald 67:54, 21 Apr 1992

May 1992

Board of Regents votes to keep football

The Board of Regents voted to keep the football program, following months of budget pressure that had prompted the ASG's February resolution of support.
